city.name: New York
city.wiki: New York and New Jersey campaign
summary: In 1776 New York was a port of about 25,000 people on the southern tip of Manhattan. Fort George guarded the harbour, Broadway ran north past Trinity Church to the Common, and the wharves of the East River were lined with warehouses and ships. Above Chambers Street lay farms, the Collect Pond and open country.

Washington fortified the town and Brooklyn Heights that spring, but in August the British landed on Long Island and beat his army there. The Americans slipped back across the East River and left Manhattan in September. Days after the British marched in, a fire burned about a quarter of the town. New York stayed the British headquarters until 1783.
city.note: Manhattan shoreline after the Ratzer Plan of 1767, and streets, buildings and fields from OpenHistoricalMap (CC0). The Brooklyn shore, the Collect Pond, the 1776 works and the extent of the Great Fire are drawn by hand from period plans. Houses between the streets are generated; surviving buildings use their real outlines.

fire.name: Burned district (Great Fire of 1776)
description: Early on 21 September 1776, six days after the British took the city, fire broke out near Whitehall Slip. A strong wind drove it north up the west side, between Broadway and the Hudson, as far as the grounds of King's College. Trinity Church burned; St Paul's Chapel was saved by men on its roof.

Some 500 houses were lost, about a quarter of the town. The British blamed rebel arsonists and hanged Nathan Hale as a spy the next day. The ruins were left as they were for the rest of the war, and a shanty town of tents and sailcloth, 'Canvas Town', grew up among them.

properties.name: Collect Pond
description: A deep spring-fed pond, the town's main source of fresh water, with tanneries, potteries and a brewery round its shores. It was filled in by 1811; the courts and Foley Square stand on the site.

properties.name: Governors Island
description: A small island off the Battery, used as a summer retreat by royal governors. Americans dug in here in April 1776 and fired on British ships; it was abandoned after the defeat on Long Island.

properties.name: Fort George
description: The fort at the tip of Manhattan, first built by the Dutch as Fort Amsterdam in 1626 and renamed for each new monarch. Its stone bastions held the governor's house and chapel; Washington's men garrisoned it in 1776 until the British took the city in September.

properties.name: The Battery
description: A stone gun platform along the water below the fort, mounting some 90 guns. It gave its name to Battery Park.

properties.name: Bowling Green
description: The town's first public park, laid out in front of the fort in 1733 and fenced with iron railings in 1771.

properties.name: Statue of George III
description: A gilded lead statue of King George III on horseback, set up on Bowling Green in 1770. On 9 July 1776, after the Declaration of Independence was read to the army, a crowd pulled it down. The lead was melted into some 42,000 musket balls.

properties.name: Trinity Church
description: The Anglican parish church of New York, built in 1698 and enlarged in 1737, with a steeple of about 175 feet facing the Hudson. It burned in the Great Fire of 21 September 1776 and stood in ruins until 1788. Today's church, the third on the site, dates from 1846.

properties.name: Trinity Churchyard
description: The burial ground round Trinity Church. Alexander Hamilton was buried here in 1804.

properties.name: St Paul's Chapel
description: A chapel of Trinity parish, opened in 1766 on the edge of town. It survived the fire of 1776 because men stood on its roof with buckets. Washington prayed here after his inauguration in 1789. It is the oldest surviving church in Manhattan; its tower and spire were added in 1794.

properties.name: City Hall
description: New York's city hall, at the head of Broad Street on Wall Street, built in 1700 to 1703. The Stamp Act Congress met here in 1765, and the Declaration of Independence was read from it on 18 July 1776. Rebuilt as Federal Hall, it saw Washington sworn in as President in 1789. The present building on the site dates from 1842.

properties.name: Fraunces Tavern
description: A merchant's house of 1719, a tavern from 1762 under Samuel Fraunces. The Sons of Liberty met here, and on 4 December 1783 Washington said farewell to his officers in its Long Room. Much rebuilt, it is now a museum.

properties.name: The Common (the Fields)
description: Open ground at the north end of town, used for grazing, militia drills and public meetings. The Sons of Liberty raised their liberty poles here, and on 9 July 1776 Washington's army formed up on it to hear the Declaration of Independence read. It is now City Hall Park.

properties.name: Liberty Pole
description: The Sons of Liberty raised a pole here to celebrate the repeal of the Stamp Act in 1766. British soldiers cut it down four times; each time a new one went up. In January 1770 a fight over it, the Battle of Golden Hill, left one man dead. The last pole stood until the British occupied the city.

properties.name: American barricades
description: Earth barricades thrown up across the streets in the spring of 1776, when Charles Lee and then Washington prepared to defend the town street by street.

properties.name: King's College
description: The colony's college, founded in 1754 and housed from 1760 in a stone building looking over the Hudson. Alexander Hamilton and John Jay studied here. In 1776 it became a military hospital. It reopened in 1784 as Columbia College.

properties.name: East River wharves
description: The port's busiest waterfront: slips and wharves from Whitehall to Catherine Street, sheltered from the ice and storms of the Hudson. Warehouses, sail lofts, markets and ropewalks crowded behind them.

properties.name: Brooklyn Ferry
description: A hamlet of taverns, storehouses and farm buildings at the ferry landing. Washington's beaten army crossed from here to Manhattan by boat on the night of 29 to 30 August 1776.

properties.name: Fort Stirling
description: The first American work on Brooklyn Heights, built in March 1776 under Lord Stirling. Its eight guns looked across the East River to the town.

properties.name: Fort Putnam
description: Fort Putnam stood on the high ground at the north end of the line. Rebuilt as Fort Greene in 1812, the site is now Fort Greene Park.

properties.name: Fort Greene
description: A star-shaped fort, the largest on the line, named after General Nathanael Greene.

properties.name: Fort Box
description: The southern fort on the line, above the marshes of Gowanus Creek.

properties.name: Cobble Hill Fort
description: A small round fort on Cobble Hill, called the Corkscrew Fort for the path that wound up to it.

properties.name: Fort Defiance
description: A battery on Red Hook that guarded the harbour channel. It fired on British ships on 27 August 1776.

properties.name: Brooklyn line
description: A mile and a half of trenches and forts across the neck of land behind Brooklyn, from Wallabout Bay to the Gowanus marshes. After the defeat on Long Island on 27 August 1776, Washington's army held this line for two days, then slipped away across the East River under cover of fog.

properties.name: St George's Chapel
description: A chapel of Trinity parish, built of stone in 1752 on Beekman Street.

properties.name: Brick Presbyterian Church
description: A Presbyterian church of 1767 facing the Common. The British used it as a prison and hospital during the occupation.

properties.name: North Dutch Church
description: The newest of the Dutch Reformed churches, opened in 1769. The British used it as a prison for American captives.

properties.name: Wall Street Presbyterian Church
description: The first Presbyterian church in the city, built on Wall Street in 1719.

properties.name: French Church
description: The Huguenot church of Saint-Esprit, built in 1704 by French Protestant refugees.

properties.name: Garden Street Dutch Church
description: The old Dutch Reformed church on Garden Street, built in 1693 when Dutch was still spoken in many New York homes.

properties.name: Mill Street Synagogue
description: Built in 1730 by Congregation Shearith Israel, the first synagogue built in North America. Most of the congregation left for Philadelphia when the British came in 1776.

Some 500 houses were lost, about a quarter of the town. The British blamed rebel arsonists and hanged Nathan Hale as a spy the next day. The ruins were left as they were for the rest of the war, and a shanty town of tents and sailcloth, 'Canvas Town', grew up among them.
